# Shōjo Manga, Japanese Gendered Language, and Queer Young Adults: What the Evidence Can and Cannot Show

As of 13 September 2026, no available study directly tests whether queer Japanese young adults who consume more shōjo manga use different first-person pronouns or sentence-ending particles in their own speech. The evidence therefore cannot establish an association, a causal effect, or a null effect. It does show that shōjo manga represents pronouns and sentence-final forms differently from prescriptive “men’s” and “women’s” language, while actual Japanese conversation—including queer interaction—contains substantial contextual, regional, age-based, and identity-based variation.

The strongest conclusion is consequently qualified. Mass media can make gendered and queer-coded speech recognizable, circulate stereotypes, and provide resources for persona construction. Queer speakers may appropriate, reject, or reinterpret those resources. But the available research does not measure shōjo exposure among a defined sample of queer Japanese young adults, nor does it connect exposure to their pronoun or particle choices.

This report first defines the population and the evidence boundaries. It then explains Japanese first-person reference and sentence-ending particles, compares shōjo manga with available benchmarks from everyday Japanese, documents what is known about queer people’s media consumption, and analyzes pronoun and particle use in queer cases. It closes by distinguishing plausible media mechanisms from claims that the evidence can actually support.

## 1. Research question, population, and evidence boundaries

### The precise question

The question has four linked components:

1. The medium is shōjo manga, not manga in general, anime, television, boys’ love, or yuri.
2. The focal population is queer Japanese young adults.
3. The outcomes are linguistic choices in personal expression: first-person pronouns and sentence-ending particles.
4. The comparison is between represented shōjo-manga language and majority use in Japanese society, followed by an assessment of whether consumption is associated with or contributes to speakers’ own usage.

These components cannot be substituted for one another. A study of shōjo characters is evidence about representation, not readership. A study of queer speakers is evidence about minority language practices, not necessarily media influence. A study of BL readers can illuminate queer-adjacent media consumption, but BL is not shōjo manga. A study of general Japanese students can provide a majority-use benchmark, but it is not a queer sample.

The available literature is therefore best treated as a set of connected but non-equivalent evidence types.

| Evidence type | Example | What it measures | What it cannot establish |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fictional corpus | Shōjo manga by [Ueno](https://linggwistiks.files.wordpress.com/2009/03/g8-linguistic-analysis-of-gender-in-manga.pdf) and [Unser-Schutz](https://jalt-publications.org/sites/default/files/pdf-article/jalt2010proc-41.pdf) | Character dialogue, genre conventions, role language | Reader uptake or personal expression |
| Everyday conversation corpus | CEJC, Sakura, NUCC, Meidai, and Fukuoka student conversations | Observed forms, frequencies, functions, addressees, and registers | Shōjo exposure or queer identity unless specifically collected |
| Queer ethnography or documentary analysis | [Abe](https://transreads.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/2021-12-30_61cdc9d64808c_QueerJapaneseGenderandSexualIdentitiesthroughLinguisticPracticesbyHidekoAbez-lib.org_.pdf), [Maree](http://intersections.anu.edu.au/issue9/maree.html), and [Bendall](https://gupea.ub.gu.se/bitstreams/5cdf108b-46a5-40d2-84e0-dfd5abc88b70/download) | Contextual queer language practices | Exposure to shōjo manga or population-wide effects |
| Media-consumption survey | [Sato and Ishida](https://files.catbox.moe/72wb58.pdf), Baudinette, and [Zsila et al.](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0198895) | Media formats, frequency, motives, and identity-related meanings | Pronoun or sentence-ending-particle adoption |
| Recognition experiment | Kinsui’s discussion of Jung’s experiment in [*Manga and Role Language Research*](https://imrc.jp/images/upload/lecture/data/Kinsui_ENG.pdf) | Recognition of fictional character types from speech | Production of those forms in everyday life |

### Who counts as queer?

There is no single operational definition across the available studies.

The 2026 Dentsu LGBTQ+ survey defines the LGBTQ+ community as everyone except respondents who identify as heterosexual and whose gender assigned at birth matches their gender identity. Its screening survey covered 46,658 Japan residents aged 20–59; 10.6% met that definition. The category includes transgender, non-binary/X-gender, questioning, gay, lesbian, bisexual/pansexual, aromantic, and asexual respondents, with overlapping identities permitted. This is a broad self-identification model, not a linguistic sample of young adults. [Dentsu’s 2026 survey](https://dentsu-ho.com/en/articles/9805)

The 2020 Dentsu survey similarly defined LGBTQ+ membership through gender assigned at birth, gender identity, and sexual orientation. Its 6,240 respondents were aged 20–59, including 555 LGBTQ+ respondents, but it did not collect shōjo exposure, pronoun use, or sentence-ending-particle use. [Dentsu’s 2020 survey](https://www.dentsu.co.jp/en/news/release/2021/0408-010371.html)

The ReBit survey reported by *The Japan Times* recruited members of Japan’s LGBTQ+ community aged 12–34 and obtained 4,733 valid responses. It is useful for establishing a broad youth context, but the available report does not provide a young-adult-only subsample or linguistic and manga-exposure measures. [ReBit survey report](https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2025/06/24/japan/japan-lgbtq-youth-survey/)

Older linguistic studies use terms and categories that do not map neatly onto contemporary LGBTQ+ identities. Abe’s 2010 work, for example, analyzes participants who identified in the source as lesbians, o-nabe, or F–M transsexuals. Maree analyzes three documentary participants who identified as onabe, while emphasizing that onabe self-identification did not necessarily mean identification as men. These categories are historically and interactionally meaningful, but they should not be silently converted into a uniform contemporary “non-binary” or “transmasculine” category.

The appropriate conclusion is that “queer” in this literature is an umbrella for several kinds of sexual, gender, and community positioning. It is not a single speech community.

### Who counts as a young adult?

The available studies also use incompatible age boundaries:

- The Sato–Ishida survey of women covered Japan residents aged 20–59.
- Its gay/bisexual-men survey had an age floor of 18 but no upper limit.
- Chen studied university students aged 20–27.
- The ReBit survey covered ages 12–34.
- Abe’s directly observed lesbian-bar employee was 20, but most of her ethnographic material does not define a young-adult sample.
- The CEJC and Sakura corpora contain college students or broad conversation samples, but do not isolate a common young-adult age band.
- Dentsu’s national surveys divide respondents into 20–39 and 40–59, which is useful for population measurement but does not define “young adult” in the focal sense.

Thus no retrieved study simultaneously restricts its participants to queer Japanese young adults and measures their shōjo consumption alongside their language. Any use of general youth, college-student, or LGBTQ+ data must remain explicitly labeled as adjacent evidence.

### What would count as direct media evidence?

A direct test would need, at minimum, an identifiable focal sample, a measurable shōjo exposure variable, and linguistic outcomes from personal expression. Relevant exposure information would include amount or frequency, age or period of access, titles and subgenres, print or digital access, and co-exposure to shōnen, josei, BL, yuri, anime, television, social media, or other media.

The linguistic data would need to distinguish:

- overt forms from subject omission;
- first-person forms such as *watashi*, *atashi*, *boku*, *ore*, *jibun*, and *uchi*;
- sentence-ending forms such as *wa*, *no*, *yo*, *ne*, *kashira*, *zo*, and *ze*;
- speaker identity and self-positioning;
- addressee relationship;
- topic and interactional function;
- formality, speech level, region, dialect, and prosody.

No retrieved study provides this combination. The absence is especially important because shōjo manga findings are usually text-corpus findings, while queer-language findings are usually small ethnographies, documentary analyses, or qualitative cases.

## 2. Japanese gendered language: pronouns and sentence-ending particles

### Gender is an indexical association, not a grammatical identity test

Japanese is often described as having gendered pronouns and gendered sentence-final particles. That description is useful as a starting point, but misleading if treated as a set of categorical grammatical rules.

A linguistic form is gender-indexical when it evokes social meanings associated with gender without directly and exclusively identifying the speaker’s sex or gender. A form can also index age, intimacy, authority, region, stance, affect, occupation, persona, or group membership. The same form may therefore produce different social meanings in different contexts.

Kinsui defines Japanese “role language” as a set of vocabulary, grammar, pronunciation, and fixed expressions that evokes attributes such as gender, age, occupation, social status, region, or race. He stresses that role language is often different from actual speech, even though Japanese speakers recognize and interpret it. [Kinsui, *Manga and Role Language Research*](https://imrc.jp/images/upload/lecture/data/Kinsui_ENG.pdf)

This distinction is central to the shōjo-manga question. A reader may recognize that a character sounds feminine, masculine, elderly, queer-coded, rough, or refined without reproducing that character’s language. Recognition, interpretation, imitation, and everyday adoption are different processes.

### First-person pronouns and self-reference

Japanese frequently omits subjects and first-person pronouns. Speakers may instead use names, kin terms, occupational titles, nicknames, or no overt self-reference at all. When a pronoun is used, it carries social and interactional information in addition to its referential meaning.

| Form | Conventional association | Common register or context | Important complication |
|---|---|---|---|
| *watakushi* | Formal for men and women | Public, formal, institutional | Can be used playfully or stylistically among intimates |
| *watashi* | Available to all; often feminine in plain speech and formal for men | Formal speech for men; broad range for women | Shared across genders and not inherently feminine |
| *atashi* | Feminine, informal | Casual interaction | Strongly associated with women in many standard-language descriptions, but actual frequency varies by age and context |
| *boku* | Masculine, relatively mild or semi-formal | Younger men, school and professional contexts | Can be used by girls and women for a “cool,” independent, or nontraditional persona |
| *ore* | Masculine, informal, sometimes rough | Close or casual interaction | Can index toughness, intimacy, anger, or a particular persona; some dialects treat *ore/ora* as gender-neutral |
| *jibun* | Relatively gender-neutral self-reference | Context-dependent; also associated with institutional or regional styles | Can be selected to avoid both feminine and masculine positioning |
| *uchi* | Regional, youthful, or casual depending on speaker and context | Especially associated with some regional and informal styles | Fictional use may signal liveliness or personality rather than a fixed gender |
| *washi* | Older male or male doctor in role language | Elderly or fictional authority figures | Actual speakers may use it regionally or humorously |

Traditional descriptions summarized by [Maree](http://intersections.anu.edu.au/issue9/maree.html), [Carpi and Iacus](https://ojcmt.editorialpark.com/download/is-japanese-gendered-language-used-on-twitter-a-large-scale-study-9141.pdf), and [Kono’s CEJC presentation](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/conversation/event/sympo6_slide_4.pdf) commonly associate *watashi/atashi* with women and *boku/ore* with men. But these are conventions and distributions, not biological rules.

The CEJC data demonstrate why omission matters. Kono extracted 2,640 possible self-reference cases from 124 conversations, excluded 201 quoted uses, and analyzed 2,439 cases. Of these, 2,212 were pronouns, 138 were kin terms, and 89 were names or nicknames. The corpus contained 449 distinct speakers and approximately 599,928 spoken words, but it was not designed around queer identity or media consumption. [Kono, “Self-reference in the CEJC”](https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/conversation/event/sympo6_slide_4.pdf)

In that corpus, *atashi* occurred 784 times among 98 speakers, including 780 female-coded cases and 4 male-coded cases. *Watashi* occurred 328 times among 96 speakers, including 271 female-coded and 57 male-coded cases. *Ore* occurred 666 times among 69 speakers, while *boku* occurred 172 times. Women in the corpus did not use *ore* or *boku* in the reported analysis. These results provide a useful majority benchmark, but they do not describe non-binary speakers, queer speakers, or shōjo readers.

Kono also found that register mattered. Female *atashi* occurred 71.3% of the time in casual conversation, 21.8% in consultation or business talk, and 6.9% in meetings. Female *watashi* showed a similar distribution: 72.7%, 21.0%, and 6.3%. Male *watashi*, by contrast, occurred 86.0% of the time in casual conversation in the reported data, showing that it was not restricted to highly formal contexts. Male *ore* also appeared in workplace conversations, although *ore* combined with polite speech was absent in the reported examples.

The study’s most important implication is methodological: pronoun choice cannot be interpreted without self-reference practices, addressee relationships, speech level, and the possibility of omission.

### Sentence-ending particles

Sentence-ending particles occur at the end of a clause and express the speaker’s attitude toward the proposition and the interlocutor. They can indicate emphasis, emotional stance, shared knowledge, agreement, uncertainty, insistence, teasing, complaint, or a request for response.

| Particle or form | Conventional gender association | Common interactional functions | Main qualification |
|---|---|---|---|
| *wa* | Rising *wa* traditionally feminine; falling *wa* often neutral or regional | Softening, emotional emphasis, personal stance, contradiction, teasing | Intonation and regional variety are decisive |
| *no* | Declarative *no* traditionally feminine; interrogative *no* often neutral | Shared knowledge, explanation, reconfirmation, new information | Declarative and interrogative uses must be separated |
| *yo* | Often neutral; sometimes masculine in combinations | Assertion, new information, emphasis | Meaning changes with intonation and combinations |
| *ne* | Broadly neutral; sometimes associated with feminine alignment | Seeking agreement, empathy, shared perspective | Common across genders and registers |
| *kashira* | Traditionally feminine | Wondering, indirect questioning, tentative request | Not more frequent among women in one large Twitter study |
| *zo*, *ze* | Masculine or rough | Strong assertion, toughness, insistence | Women use them in some contexts and communities |
| *na*, *sa*, *kana* | Mixed, masculine, or neutral depending on form and region | Reflection, assertion, wondering, informal alignment | Large variation by age, dialect, and discourse context |
| *yo ne*, *da yo*, *da yo ne* | Often neutral or weakly gendered in actual use | Confirmation, rapport, emphasis, shared information | Frequently used across genders |

Abe reports that *yo*, *da yo*, and *da yo ne* were the most frequent sentence-ending forms in the lesbian bars she observed. The forms could create directness and intimacy without asserting a male identity. A customer’s use of *da yo* in “Kore otoko da yo” was interpreted as neutral in that speaker’s context rather than as straightforward masculine speech. [Abe, *Queer Japanese*](https://transreads.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/2021-12-30_61cdc9d64808c_QueerJapaneseGenderandSexualIdentitiesthroughLinguisticPracticesbyHidekoAbez-lib.org_.pdf)

The particle *wa* is especially important because its written form conceals prosody. Rising Tokyo *wa* has traditionally been associated with a soft feminine style. Falling *wa* is associated with Kansai speech and can be gender-neutral. The same written sentence can therefore receive different gender interpretations depending on region and intonation. [Tofugu’s summary of queer Japanese](https://www.tofugu.com/japanese/queer-japanese/) and [Aizawa’s manga analysis](http://www.urayasu.meikai.ac.jp/japanese/meikainihongo/8/aizawa.pdf) both illustrate this problem.

The 2023 *Languages* study of young college students found that *wa* was produced more often by male than female speakers in its corpus: 43 of 68 tokens, or 63%, were produced by male-coded speakers and 25, or 37%, by female-coded speakers. Declarative *no* occurred 84 times, with 56% of tokens produced by male-coded speakers and 44% by female-coded speakers. The study excluded interrogative *no* and double-final-particle combinations and did not rigorously analyze prosody, so these figures are not universal gender rates. [“A Study of *wa* and *no* in Youth Conversations”](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-471X/8/3/222)

The point is not that *wa* and *no* are “really masculine.” It is that their interactional functions allow them to be used by speakers whose identity does not match the stereotype attached to the form.

### Historical construction of gendered language

The contemporary system of gender-indexical language is historically produced rather than timeless.

Ueno argues that modern Japanese women’s language was constructed through late-Meiji domestic novels and subsequently circulated through letters and advice columns in girls’ and young women’s magazines. Forms associated with softness, refinement, and nonassertiveness acquired ideological meanings connected to the ideal of the “good wife, wise mother.” [Ueno, “Shōjo and Adult Women”](https://linggwistiks.files.wordpress.com/2009/03/g8-linguistic-analysis-of-gender-in-manga.pdf)

Kinsui’s historical account adds a different layer. In Edo-period literary materials, forms such as *ore* and *ze* could be used by characters of more than one gender. During the Meiji period, schoolboys’ language helped consolidate *boku*, while schoolgirls’ language circulated forms such as *da wa*, *kashira*, and *te yo*. Popular magazines then helped spread *josei kotoba* across regions and social groups. [Kinsui, *Manga and Role Language Research*](https://imrc.jp/images/upload/lecture/data/Kinsui_ENG.pdf)

These accounts are compatible if read as a history of reclassification. Earlier forms were not necessarily gender-exclusive; modernization, schooling, print circulation, and language ideology increasingly attached them to particular social images. What later appeared to be “women’s language” or “men’s language” was partly the result of historical enregisterment: repeated association between forms and recognizable personae.

Nakamura similarly traces modern gendered first-person pronouns to the Meiji construction of standardized national language, in which male-appropriate forms were treated as legitimate *kokugo* and female alternatives became associated with femininity. Her account emphasizes that speakers can break these norms to perform new identities. [Nakamura, “Japanese Gendered First-Person Pronouns”](https://eall.columbian.gwu.edu/japanese-gendered-first-person-pronouns-norms-and-innovation-identity-works)

The historical lesson is relevant to media influence but does not prove a direct reader effect. Print and broadcast media can circulate a form, attach social meanings to it, and make it recognizable. They do not thereby determine how an individual reader will speak.

## 3. Shōjo manga language and the majority-use comparison

### What the shōjo corpora actually contain

Shōjo manga is a market category aimed primarily at girls from elementary school through high school. Ueno distinguishes it from ladies’ manga, which is marketed to adult women and more often addresses careers, divorce, family relations, and other adult social concerns. [Ueno](https://linggwistiks.files.wordpress.com/2009/03/g8-linguistic-analysis-of-gender-in-manga.pdf)

This distinction matters because “women’s manga” cannot be treated as a single exposure. A corpus of teenage romance manga, a corpus of adult women’s manga, a yuri title, and a BL title may represent different personae, audiences, and linguistic strategies.

Ueno analyzed nine magazines published in 2003 and 2004: four shōjo magazines—*Nakayoshi*, *Ribon*, *Hana to Yume*, and *The Margaret*—and five ladies’ magazines. The analysis used complete utterances by female characters, focused on informal dialogue, and excluded formal conversations because formal Japanese reduces many gendered grammatical differences.

Her shōjo corpus showed strong age differentiation:

| Female character age | Feminine forms | Masculine forms | Neutral forms |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Teens | 23.5% | 24.3% | 52.2% |
| Twenties | 54.9% | 9.8% | 35.3% |
| Thirty and older | 58.7% | 5.5% | 33.8% |

These percentages are sums of Ueno’s strongly and moderately feminine categories and strongly and moderately masculine categories. Among teenagers, the individual figures were 8.4% strongly feminine, 15.1% moderately feminine, 4.1% strongly masculine, 20.2% moderately masculine, and 52.2% neutral. Among characters in their twenties, strongly feminine forms alone accounted for 37.6%, while neutral forms accounted for 35.3%. Among characters aged thirty and above, strongly feminine forms accounted for 33.9%, moderately feminine forms for 24.8%, and neutral forms for 33.8%.

The direction is clear within the fictional corpus: teenage shōjo characters were represented with a high proportion of neutral and moderately masculine forms, while older female characters were represented with more conventional feminine forms. Ueno interprets this partly as an index of youth and partly as an escape from adult gender obligations. It does not mean that real adolescent girls or queer young adults used the same proportions.

Unser-Schutz provides a second, more extensive corpus. It analyzed the first three volumes of eight popular titles—four shōjo and four shōnen series—totalling 579,261 characters in 45,073 entries. The shōjo titles were *Kimi ni Todoke*, *Nana*, *Nodame Cantabile*, and *Rabu-Kon*; *Rabu-Kon* uses Kansai dialect. Titles were selected through sales rankings and a survey of high-school students’ manga-reading habits, but the study did not recruit readers or measure individual exposure. [Unser-Schutz](https://jalt-publications.org/sites/default/files/pdf-article/jalt2010proc-41.pdf)

### First-person pronouns in shōjo dialogue

In the shōjo portion of Unser-Schutz’s corpus, male characters produced 563 first-person-pronoun tokens. *Ore* accounted for 445, or 79.04%; *watashi* for 68, or 12.08%; *boku* for 41, or 7.28%; and *atashi* for 7, or 1.24%. Female characters produced 584 tokens: *atashi* accounted for 435, or 73.98%; *watashi* for 146, or 24.83%; *watakushi* for 2, or 0.34%; and *washi* for 1, or 0.17%. No female character in this shōjo subset used *ore* or *boku* as a first-person pronoun.

Across the complete eight-title corpus, male characters’ most common first-person form was *ore* at 62.32% of male-character pronoun tokens. Female characters used *atashi* at 54.81% and *watashi* at 43.48%. The corpus contained 183 occurrences of *jibun* but no clearly identifiable first-person use, and 63 occurrences of *uchi* but only four clear first-person uses.

These figures challenge two opposite assumptions. First, shōjo manga does not simply expose female readers to female characters using masculine first-person pronouns. Second, a female character’s use of *atashi* or *watashi* does not show that the character is intended as a sociolinguistically realistic model. These are fictional distributions organized by genre, character role, and narrative design.

A separate 2010 abstract examining six popular manga series likewise reported that no female characters used masculine first-person pronouns and that only a few female characters used masculine second-person pronouns. The abstract explicitly states that the relationship between manga and language use remained unclear because previous work had not adequately examined pronoun distributions in manga. [Unser-Schutz, LSA abstract](https://doi.org/10.3765/exabs.v0i0.514)

Kloutvorová’s later analysis of fictional teenage girls in shōjo manga also found relatively limited first-person variety. *Watashi* and *atashi* were the most frequent forms, while role language used to mark a sharply specific character type was limited. Frequent *uchi* use in some characters was interpreted as casual speech by active, lively, vigorous personalities rather than as a stable gender role. [Kloutvorová](https://docslib.org/doc/8620122/teenage-girls-and-female-sh%C5%8Djo-manga-characters)

The shōjo pronoun pattern is therefore not a single “manga language.” It includes a conservative allocation of *ore* and *boku* to male characters, frequent *atashi* and *watashi* for female characters, and subject omission. It also varies by age and persona.

### Sentence-ending particles in shōjo dialogue

Unser-Schutz’s sentence-final-particle categories show a sharper shōjo–shōnen contrast than the pronoun data.

For male shōjo characters, 33.39% of SFP tokens were categorized as mildly masculine, 27.31% as strongly masculine, 32.87% as neutral, 4.53% as mildly feminine, and 1.89% as strongly feminine. For female shōjo characters, 42.42% were neutral, 28.11% mildly masculine, 13.47% moderately feminine, 9.18% strongly feminine, and 6.81% strongly masculine.

Thus, female shōjo characters’ neutral and mildly masculine categories together comprised 70.53% of their SFP tokens, while strongly and moderately feminine forms together comprised 22.65%. This is a substantial divergence from a prescriptive model in which female characters should overwhelmingly use feminine forms. It is not, however, a measured divergence from real Japanese society because the study did not use a matched everyday-conversation control group.

The contrast with female characters in shōnen manga is striking. Female shōnen characters used strongly feminine forms for 45.64% of their SFP tokens, moderately feminine forms for 19.16%, neutral forms for 17.13%, mildly masculine forms for 16.82%, and strongly masculine forms for 1.25%. Genre therefore affected fictional gender representation: shōjo presented female characters with more neutral and mildly masculine speech, while shōnen more often used strongly feminine role language for female characters.

Ueno’s analysis points in the same direction but adds narrative context. In shōjo manga, strongly feminine particles were used when a character emphasized femininity, displayed a noble background, entered a semi-formal situation, or represented an older woman. Strongly masculine forms appeared rarely and often in anger, confrontation, authority, or a boyish persona. Neutral and moderately masculine forms appeared throughout teenage peer interaction.

The shōjo pattern can therefore be summarized as follows:

- teenage girls are represented with a broad range of forms;
- neutral and moderately masculine endings are common;
- strongly feminine forms are contextually marked rather than uniformly distributed;
- older female characters are more strongly associated with conventional femininity;
- masculine-coded forms often index anger, assertiveness, maturity, authority, or a particular persona.

This is not evidence that readers adopt those forms. It is evidence that shōjo manga presents gender as narratively and interactionally variable.

### Aizawa’s diachronic shōjo comparison

Aizawa examined nine sentence-ending forms in three shōjo manga with female middle- or high-school protagonists:

- *Glass Mask*, serialized 1976–1979;
- *Tokimeki Tonight*, serialized 1982–1986;
- *Boys Over Flowers*, using source volumes from 1996–1998.

The nine forms were *wa*, *dawa*, *yo*, *ne*, *no ne*, *wane*, *kashira*, *mono*, and non-interrogative *no*. Raw totals across the nine categories declined from 840 in *Glass Mask* to 494 in *Tokimeki Tonight* and 292 in *Boys Over Flowers*. The raw count of *wa* fell from 249 to 145 to 44, while *dawa* fell from 79 to 29 to 18.

Other forms changed unevenly. *Yo* declined from 161 to 101 to 61; *ne* from 69 to 34 to 23; *no ne* from 22 to 18 to 2; *kashira* from 68 to 34 to 16; and *wane* from 56 to 43 to 12. *Mono* remained comparatively stable at 23, 29, and 25, while non-interrogative *no* fell from 113 to 61 and rose again to 91.

These results suggest a decline in several traditionally feminine forms, but raw counts cannot establish a normalized rate of change because the titles differ in length, narrative structure, and number of relevant utterances. They also cannot establish a change in readers’ speech.

Aizawa’s examples further undermine categorical gender labels. In *Boys Over Flowers*, *da yo* appeared commonly in both male and female dialogue. Male characters used *wa* in three examples, including “*Ore ie deru wa*” (“I’m leaving the house”), but Aizawa could not determine whether these represented Kansai dialect or falling, low-pitched *wa*. Written manga does not supply the prosody needed to decide.

### Majority-use benchmarks from actual Japanese

The available majority benchmarks do not form one representative national corpus. They nevertheless allow a comparison on shared axes.

#### Pronouns

The CEJC findings differ from the shōjo corpus in both distribution and unit of analysis. Fictional shōjo female characters used *atashi* for 73.98% of their first-person-pronoun tokens and *watashi* for 24.83%, with no *ore* or *boku*. In the CEJC, female-coded speakers produced 780 *atashi* tokens and 271 *watashi* tokens, while male-coded speakers produced 57 *watashi* tokens and 666 *ore* tokens. The source does not provide a directly comparable female-only denominator for every possible self-reference form, and the two corpora differ in period, setting, and speaker status.

The difference is nevertheless analytically useful. Shōjo dialogue makes character gender and role legible through concentrated pronoun choices. Everyday conversation contains the same inventory but uses pronouns less consistently, with omission, names, kin terms, and shifts across settings playing a larger role.

#### Sentence-ending particles

The Fukuoka student corpus analyzed by Chen contains 3,603 utterances from 25 university students aged 20–27: 16 male-coded and 9 female-coded participants. The conversations were collected between December 2007 and August 2008 in a national-university student dormitory. The study considered region, formality, hierarchy, intimacy, and interactional context. [Chen](https://api.lib.kyushu-u.ac.jp/opac_download_md/4494703/029_p061.pdf)

Chen’s observed distributions differed from conventional classifications. Forms in an almost-male group included *daro*, *yaro*, *noka*, and *zo*. A female-higher group included *yone*, *yo*, *da yo*, *da yo ne*, and *ka*. A near-equal group included *kane*, *desho*, *noyo*, *none*, *ze*, *yana*, *kana*, *dana*, and *yan*, with male–female usage-rate differences of no more than 0.2 percentage points.

Most forms declined as formality increased. Women’s use of forms associated with men was concentrated in informal interactions and was rare with superiors or socially distant interlocutors. Regional background mattered: all four female *yaro* examples came from Kyushu-born participants, all four female falling-*wa* examples came from Osaka-born participants, and all three female *yona* examples came from Osaka-born participants.

Chen’s qualitative examples show that *yone* and *ne* can seek agreement and solidarity. In one exchange, two close female dorm residents used *yone/ne* three times across four utterances to confirm a shared evaluation. In another, *none* framed information as shared knowledge and softened the claim. These functions are not reducible to “female grammar.”

The 2023 Sakura study provides a more recent college-student comparison. Its corpus contains 18 video-recorded conversations, with 14 selected for analysis. The selected conversations involved native college students in close relationships who mainly used casual forms. The study reported 24 male-coded and 13 female-coded speakers, although the corpus design involved repeated participants. Sexual orientation, gender identity, and geography were unavailable. [Languages study](https://www.mdpi.com/2226-471X/8/3/222)

In Sakura, male-coded speakers produced 43 of 68 *wa* tokens, or 63%, while female-coded speakers produced 25, or 37%. Male-coded speakers also produced 56% of 84 declarative *no* tokens, compared with 44% for female-coded speakers. Twelve of the 43 male *wa* tokens and 9 of the 25 female *wa* tokens followed emotion-denoting adjectives. The study interpreted male *wa* as emphasizing personal emotion, opinion, decision, or stance. Six cases involved young men teasing female addressees, with laughter marking the interaction as non-serious and intimate.

Fukao’s analysis of the Meidai Conversation Corpus offers a larger historical benchmark. The corpus contains 129 conversations collected in 2001–2003, approximately 100 hours of speech, and 198 participants—161 women and 37 men. It identified 1,026 *wa*-class tokens among women and 135 among men. Women aged 10–50 used *wa*-class forms at rates of roughly 70–80%, while 94% of women aged 60 and above used at least one. Notably, 67% of men in their twenties used *wa*-class forms. [Fukao](https://www.jstage.jst.go.jp/article/nihongokyoiku/173/0/173_31/_pdf)

Fukao classified 621 sentence-final *wa* tokens into nine sentence types. Young speakers used *wa* not only for emotion and personal judgment but also for correction, disagreement, empathy, joking, and playful interaction. This differs from the older stereotype of *wa* as a uniformly soft feminine ending.

Jia’s comparison of the Showa Speech Corpus, NUCC, and CEJC further shows why a single majority rate would be misleading. The study examined 5,570 cases of *yo* and *ne* following nouns, adverbs, and na-adjectives across three periods: 1952–1969, 2001–2003, and 2016–2020. Gender differences were significant for several combinations in the historical corpus, absent in all reported NUCC combinations, and significant for only some combinations in CEJC. The direction depended on particle, preceding part of speech, and period. [Jia](https://pdf.hanspub.org/ml20240100000_96439715.pdf)

#### Social media as a contemporary but non-equivalent benchmark

Carpi and Iacus analyzed 408 million Japanese tweets from 2015–2019 and a manually classified sample of 2,355 Twitter accounts. They extracted 26,737,077 tweets containing 29 sentence-final particles or 8 first-person pronouns, approximately 6% of the repository. They report that gendered forms occur on Twitter but that prescriptive classifications frequently fail.

In the manually classified account sample, *watashi* and *atashi* were more frequent among female-coded accounts, while *ore* and *boku* were mostly associated with male-coded accounts. But *kashira*, conventionally strongly feminine, was not more common among female accounts. *Jan* was approximately equal across groups, and the data showed movement toward neutral forms. The account coding used apparent binary gender categories and did not identify queer or non-binary speakers.

Twitter is not face-to-face speech, but its immediate audience and response structure can make it more interactional than conventional writing. It should therefore be treated as a mediated personal-expression benchmark, not as a direct substitute for conversation.

### The comparison on shared axes

| Axis | Shōjo fictional dialogue | Available majority-use evidence | Resulting judgment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pronoun inventory | Female characters favor *atashi/watashi*; female *ore/boku* is absent or rare in the cited corpora | Everyday speakers use *atashi, watashi, ore,* and *boku*, with omission and shifting | The inventory overlaps, but manga assigns forms more tightly to character roles |
| SFP distribution | Teenage female characters show high neutral and mildly masculine proportions; older characters use more feminine forms | Actual speech shows cross-gender *wa/no*, declining or context-specific feminine forms, and strong regional effects | Shōjo diverges from prescriptive stereotypes, but a single shōjo–society effect size is unavailable |
| Speaker or character identity | Gender, age, personality, authority, romance, and narrative role are deliberately designed | Identity, stance, age, intimacy, occupation, and addressee jointly shape use | Character gender is a representational device; speaker identity is negotiated in interaction |
| Register and context | Mostly informal fictional dialogue; prosody often unavailable | Casual, workplace, dormitory, social-media, and mixed-formality contexts are separately observable | Direct comparisons require matched register and prosody |
| Historical period and region | 1970s–1990s titles, 2003–2004 magazines, and 2010 corpus | Conversation corpora range from 1952 to 2020; dialect and cohort differ | Apparent differences may reflect period, genre, or region rather than media influence |

The comparison supports a partial but important answer. Shōjo manga has a recognizable pattern: it often presents teenage female characters with neutral or mildly masculine sentence endings and with a broad range of stances, while allocating strongly masculine first-person pronouns mainly to male characters. Actual Japanese conversation also departs from categorical gender stereotypes, but it does so through interactional functions, regional forms, addressee relationships, and speaker-specific choices.

What the evidence does not provide is a matched, same-period, same-region, same-register comparison that would quantify the divergence between shōjo dialogue and majority societal speech. The direction of divergence is partly visible; its general size is not.

### Media circulation, recognition, and uptake

There are strong reasons to regard media as relevant to language ideology.

Kinsui reports that 93 of 273 examples in his *Glossary of Role Language* were drawn from manga, with 39 including reproduced manga images. He also describes a 2007 experiment in which native Japanese participants reinserted dialogue into manga panels after the images and lines had been separated. Native Japanese participants matched the lines correctly in 70.2% of responses, rising to 89.6% when only Japanese manga was used. Korean participants scored 42.8% overall, 44.4% with Japanese manga, and 41.2% with Korean manhwa. The experiment demonstrates shared recognition of Japanese manga role language, not production by readers.

The historical evidence is similar. Ueno argues that print media helped construct and circulate women’s language, while Kinsui shows how manga helped establish elderly-male role language through recurring characters such as Dr. Ochanomizu in *Astro Boy*. These are examples of diffusion and social legibility. They are not longitudinal demonstrations that readers adopted the forms in personal speech.

Fukao explicitly speculates that television variety programs may have helped spread a forceful or humorous use of *wa* from Kansai performers to younger speakers in eastern Japan. The proposed mechanism is that emotionally salient forms are repeated, captioned, and memorable. The article labels this an inference, not an exposure-tested causal result. It concerns television and *wa*, not shōjo manga and queer young adults.

The evidence therefore supports a layered media model:

1. Media can repeat and circulate forms.
2. Repetition can attach social meanings to those forms.
3. Audiences can recognize the meanings.
4. Some readers or viewers may selectively appropriate the forms.
5. Uptake depends on identity, peer practice, context, region, and the speaker’s desired persona.

Only the first three steps are directly documented for the relevant Japanese role-language systems. The fourth and fifth are plausible but untested for the focal population and outcomes.

## 4. Queer Japanese young adults’ shōjo-manga consumption

### No direct focal consumption study

No retrieved study reports individual-level shōjo consumption among queer Japanese young adults together with pronoun or sentence-ending-particle data.

The available shōjo sources describe texts:

- Ueno analyzes four shōjo magazines published in 2003–2004.
- Unser-Schutz analyzes four shōjo series and the first three volumes of each.
- Aizawa analyzes three historical shōjo titles.
- Kloutvorová analyzes fictional teenage-girl characters.
- The six-series pronoun study analyzes fictional manga lines.

None of these sources reports whether queer Japanese young adults read the titles, how often they read them, when they encountered them, whether they read print or digital editions, or what other media they consumed.

The available readership evidence is either general youth data or adjacent genres.

### Adjacent Japanese surveys

The 2021 Sato–Ishida report contains two Japanese web surveys, but neither is a shōjo-reader language study.

The women’s-monitor survey recruited Japan residents registered as female aged 20–59. It obtained 1,524 valid responses and attempted to balance four cells: readers and non-readers in their twenties and thirties, and readers and non-readers in their forties and fifties. “BL reader” meant selecting BL as a hobby and reporting that they had often or somewhat enjoyed BL content during the preceding three years. The sample was not representative, and approximately three quarters of respondents identified as heterosexual.

The gay/bisexual-men survey recruited through the 9monsters dating application. It obtained 4,041 valid responses, with an age floor of 18 and no upper limit; 2,538 were classified as BL readers. Approximately 60% of respondents were aged 39 or younger and 40% were aged 40 or older. BL readers had a mean age of 34.8, compared with 39.8 among non-readers. The researchers explicitly warn that app recruitment and the different age structures prevent generalization to Japanese gay or bisexual men as a whole. [Sato and Ishida](https://files.catbox.moe/72wb58.pdf)

The report provides useful information about media format. Among 782 female-monitor BL readers, 95% selected manga, approximately half selected novels and anime, and 15–25% selected drama, film, or games. Among 2,538 gay/bisexual-men BL readers, 88% selected manga, 44% drama, 40% film, and 25% novels.

These results show that queer-adjacent media consumption is cross-media rather than isolated. They do not show shōjo exposure. They also do not measure language. A reader who consumes BL manga, anime, television drama, and film cannot be treated as a shōjo-only reader.

The gay/bisexual-men survey also asked about gay-oriented manga during the preceding three years. Of all 4,041 respondents, 37% said they had read such manga often, 29% somewhat, 18% not much, 12% not in the previous three years but earlier, and 4% neither recently nor earlier. Again, the exposure is gay-oriented manga, not shōjo.

The report does, however, demonstrate a possible route from media to personal meaning. Among its gay/bisexual-men BL readers, 56% said BL always or often gave form to their own desires, 64% said it gave form to relationships they wished existed, and 67% said they could enjoy it with little stress. These are self-reported interpretive and affective responses, not evidence of adopting pronouns or particles.

Baudinette’s 2018 chapter similarly examines how media consumption informs young Japanese gay men’s understandings of desire and identity. The accessible record identifies a focus group concerning *Otooto no Otto*, but it does not provide extractable findings about shōjo, pronoun use, sentence-final particles, or causal uptake. [Baudinette](https://www.academia.edu/36157601/_Finding_the_Law_through_Creating_and_Consuming_Gay_Manga_in_Japan_From_Heteronormativity_to_Queer_Activism)

### Other manga genres are not interchangeable

Yuri and BL are relevant because they may overlap with queer media communities, but they are not interchangeable with shōjo.

Maser’s 2015 study examined ten milestone yuri texts from the 1910s to the 2010s, interviewed ten manga-magazine editors, and obtained 1,352 completed questionnaires from Japanese yuri fans. Its principal concern was genre formation and fan interpretation, not pronoun or sentence-final-particle use. The retrieved findings do not identify a queer-young-adult-only sample or an exposure measure tied to personal expression. [Maser](http://ubt.opus.hbz-nrw.de/volltexte/2015/944)

Reported yuri readership is also heterogeneous. A secondary account gives different readership profiles for *Yuri Hime* and *Yuri Hime S* across periods, and a 1,352-person survey classified respondents through sex and preferred-lover categories rather than a direct queer-identity measure. These figures cannot be treated as a representative sample of queer Japanese young-adult shōjo readers.

BL has a specific historical relationship to shōjo: male–male romance fiction emerged in the 1970s as a subgenre associated with shōjo culture, but contemporary BL is a distinct set of commercial and fan practices. [Zsila et al.](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0198895) describe this history and distinguish the broader yaoi/BL media field from ordinary shōjo romance.

### Exposure measures from non-Japanese research

Zsila and colleagues provide a useful example of how exposure can be measured, though their study is not Japanese and not about shōjo. Their voluntary online survey recruited 724 yaoi consumers aged 18–73 through a Hungarian news website. Participants reported whether they consumed yaoi occasionally or at least monthly, and reported age at first exposure.

In that sample, 71.13% consumed yaoi occasionally during the previous year and 28.87% monthly or more frequently. Mean age at first exposure was 13.77 years, with a standard deviation of 7.82. Frequent consumption was more common among non-heterosexual than heterosexual respondents—36.4% versus 24.6%—but the association was small, with \(\Phi=0.13\). The study did not examine Japanese-language use, shōjo, or personal pronouns.

Its value here is methodological rather than substantive: frequency, timing, identity, and age can be measured separately. The Japanese shōjo literature has not done this for the focal population.

### General readership data

A May 2020 LINE Research survey of Japanese high-school students distinguished shōjo manga, aimed at girls, from josei manga, aimed at women. The retrieved result describes the female share only as “almost ** percent,” with the numeric value masked, and gives no queer subgroup, exposure frequency, title information, or language outcome. It cannot establish a focal readership rate. [LINE Research result](https://www.statista.com/statistics/1214343/japan-reader-share-female-targeted-manga-high-school-students-by-gender/)

More general manga-readership data also require caution because print readership and digital consumption are increasingly separate. A secondary report drawing on National Association of School Librarians surveys describes declines in regular manga-magazine readership among Japanese schoolchildren, while noting that digital manga and app-based consumption complicate the interpretation. These figures concern general youth and manga magazines, not queer young adults or shōjo-language effects. [Unseen Japan](https://unseen-japan.com/japanese-teens-manga-readership-decline/)

The exposure record can therefore be summarized precisely:

- shōjo texts and titles are documented;
- general youth readership is incompletely documented;
- BL consumption among adjacent Japanese populations is documented;
- queer media consumption and identity meanings are documented in some studies;
- queer Japanese young-adult shōjo exposure is not directly documented;
- no study links exposure dose to pronoun or sentence-final-particle use.

## 5. Pronoun use in queer personal expression

### Queer speakers do not form one pronoun system

The strongest direct evidence comes from small, contextualized cases. These cases are valuable precisely because they reveal how pronouns operate in interaction, but they cannot be generalized into a community-wide frequency distribution.

### Abe’s panel discussion

Abe analyzes a transcript from the bisexual and lesbian magazine *Anise* involving six self-identified panelists: two F–M transsexuals, two o-nabe, and two lesbians. In that panel, the two transsexual participants used *boku*, the two o-nabe used *jibun*, and the lesbians used *watashi* almost uniformly.

The pattern is not a general rule about those identities. It belongs to one magazine panel, one topic, one audience, and one interactional setting. Abe interprets the forms as different appropriations of available masculine or neutral resources. The fact that the transsexual panelists used *boku* and the o-nabe used *jibun* does not tell us whether they used the same forms at work, with family, in bars, or with intimate partners. [Abe](https://transreads.org/wp-content/uploads/2021/12/2021-12-30_61cdc9d64808c_QueerJapaneseGenderandSexualIdentitiesthroughLinguisticPracticesbyHidekoAbez-lib.org_.pdf)

### One lesbian-bar employee: *jibun* and *ore*

Abe’s most revealing example concerns a 20-year-old lesbian-bar employee who had worked at the bar for almost a year. In conversation with Abe, who was a relatively new researcher-customer, the employee used *jibun*. After more than two hours of face-to-face interaction, the employee spoke by telephone with a regular customer and shifted to *ore*. In the same call she used *omē* in anger and *anta* while persuading the customer. Formal *anata* was almost never used in the bar; speakers often preferred nicknames or first names.

Abe interprets *jibun* as a public or expected face and *ore* as a more intimate, emotionally exposed face. The shift is not explained by a change in sex or fixed gender identity. It tracks addressee, familiarity, emotion, and register.

This case is especially relevant to a media-influence argument because it demonstrates that an overtly masculine pronoun can be selected for interactional reasons. If a listener hears *ore* in a queer context, the form may index anger, toughness, intimacy, or a particular persona rather than a male identity acquired from a manga character.

### The onabe cases in *Shinjuku Boys*

Maree analyzes the 1995 documentary *Shinjuku Boys*, which follows three Club Marilyn hosts in Tokyo: Kazuki, Gaishi, and Tatsu. All identify as onabe, but Maree emphasizes that onabe self-identification does not necessarily mean identification as men. The documentary is a three-person media corpus, not a representative young-adult sample. [Maree](http://intersections.anu.edu.au/issue9/maree.html)

Gaishi uses *ore* and *jibun* for self-reference in all of his on-camera interactions. *Ore* occurs most often when he discusses gender. When a customer presses him to say whether he considers himself a man, Gaishi replies with *ore wa ore dakara*—“because I’m me”—and then says he does not think of himself as either a girl or a man.

The form *ore* therefore performs a complex positioning. It invokes a masculine resource while rejecting a simple male identity. Maree further observes that Gaishi uses *ore* in discussions of gender and in contexts involving a girlfriend, but uses the more neutral *jibun* when discussing sexual experiences or his body. The contrast suggests that the choice depends on which aspect of self is being made relevant.

This is not evidence of manga influence. It is evidence that queer speakers can use a form associated with masculinity to construct a “not-girl,” “not-feminine,” or personally assertive position without accepting the social identity conventionally associated with the form.

### A contemporary documentary sample

Bendall’s 2021 thesis analyzes speech in the 2019 documentary *Queer Japan* and compares it with Abe’s earlier research. Its 32 subjects include men, women, transgender people, and unspecified or more difficult-to-classify identities; many are described as being in their thirties and forties. This is closer to contemporary queer speech than a general college corpus, but it is still a documentary sample shaped by selection, interview context, and the observer’s paradox. [Bendall, *Queer Japanese*](https://gupea.ub.gu.se/bitstreams/5cdf108b-46a5-40d2-84e0-dfd5abc88b70/download)

Bendall reports that 23 of 32 subjects used no first-person pronoun in their analyzed segments. Among the nine subjects who used one, *watashi* accounted for six uses and *boku* for three. No *ore* or *atashi* was reported in the table. One *watashi* entry came from subtitles for a woman using Japanese Sign Language, so the thesis marks that case as uncertain with respect to spoken Japanese.

The result is consistent with two broader facts:

1. subject omission is common in Japanese;
2. queer identity does not produce a single alternative pronoun distribution.

The same thesis reports variation in formality. Four men used only formal language, three only informal language, two shifted from formal to informal, and two mixed levels. Among women, four used only formal language, none used only informal language, one decreased in formality, and two mixed levels. The author interprets the pattern as partly related to the documentary crew and changing familiarity, not simply gender.

### A counterexample to automatic media influence

A first-person account published by LGBTER describes a queer narrator who began using *boku* in late elementary school because *watashi* felt intensely aversive. The narrator explicitly says this was not caused by manga or anime. Parents, relatives, and teachers corrected the usage, and the narrator stopped using *boku* after entering middle school when peers associated a girl using it with an otaku identity. [LGBTER NOISE](https://lgbter.jp/noise/0088/)

This is one person’s retrospective account, not a population estimate. Its analytical value is that it shows an alternative pathway: identity discomfort, institutional correction, and peer policing can shape pronoun use without the speaker attributing the choice to media.

### Age-adjacent evidence from girls’ speech

Miyazaki’s longitudinal ethnography at a Japanese junior high school is not a queer study and does not measure shōjo exposure. It nevertheless provides important counterevidence to a simple “masculine pronouns equal male identity or manga imitation” model.

Girls at Sakura Junior High School used *ore* and *boku*. They associated *ore* with being cool, powerful, independent, and assertive, and treated *boku* as acceptable for girls while evaluating boys who used it as weak or childish. Miyazaki found no evidence that the girls wanted to become boys. Their use created a positive *ore* persona for girl users and a local register in which masculine forms could produce social capital. [Miyazaki](https://doi.org/10.1515/ijsl-2022-0093)

The same mechanism could operate in queer speech, but it need not originate in manga. A form can be learned from media, community interaction, peer practice, regional speech, or the speaker’s own metapragmatic reinterpretation.

### Pronouns: comparison and judgment

The relevant comparison is not “shōjo uses feminine pronouns, queer people use masculine pronouns.” The evidence is more complex:

- shōjo female characters in the cited corpora overwhelmingly use *atashi* and *watashi*;
- male characters use *ore* and *boku*;
- queer speakers use *watashi, boku, ore,* and *jibun* in context-specific ways;
- actual Japanese speakers frequently omit pronouns;
- queer speakers may use a gender-indexed form while rejecting the identity stereotype attached to it;
- pronoun choice can shift with addressee, intimacy, emotional stance, topic, and persona.

The direct evidence supports within-group variation and context-sensitive self-presentation. It does not support a shōjo-exposure association among queer Japanese young adults. No focal study reports that high shōjo consumers use more *watashi*, more *atashi*, more *boku*, more *ore*, or fewer omitted subjects than low consumers.

## 6. Sentence-ending particles in queer personal expression

### Queer interaction makes the limits of gender labels visible

Sentence-ending particles are particularly revealing because their meanings depend heavily on prosody and interaction. A pronoun may be recognizable as a self-reference form, but a particle’s social effect can change with intonation, timing, addressee, sequence position, and stance.

### Abe’s lesbian-bar speech

Abe reports that *yo*, *da yo*, and *da yo ne* were the most frequent sentence-ending forms in the lesbian bars she observed. Traditional classifications call rising *wa*, *na no*, *na no ne*, and *kashira* feminine, and *zo*, *ze*, *da*, and *da yo* masculine. But Abe’s observations show that speakers can use the latter forms to construct directness, solidarity, and in-group intimacy.

A bar customer used *da yo* in “Kore otoko da yo” (“This is a man”), and Abe interpreted the form as neutral in context. The form did not index a male identity. It helped produce a direct, informal style among lesbian interlocutors and could treat another queer woman as an in-group member.

This use is compatible with a community practice in which masculine-coded particles signal toughness or intimacy rather than heterosexual masculinity. It is not a norm for all lesbian speakers, and Abe explicitly cautions that practices vary by bar and situation.

### Maree’s *no* as group authority

Maree’s analysis of Kazuki in *Shinjuku Boys* provides a different example. In the documentary’s traditional classification, neutral forms were most frequent for all three onabe hosts, followed by masculine and then feminine forms. Kazuki’s masculine and feminine forms were relatively evenly distributed.

Kazuki used declarative *no* while explaining Club Marilyn’s dress code and customer-relations norms to Sampei, a new host. In one sequence, upward-intimated *no* functions as a neutral question; falling *no* expresses mild insistence. Maree interprets *no* not as femininity but as a group-authority marker: it frames the relevant knowledge as shared among Club Marilyn hosts, draws Sampei into that group, creates rapport, and exercises authority.

The same particle is therefore capable of indexing group membership and shared knowledge rather than feminine identity. Its social meaning emerges from the workplace hierarchy and the interactional sequence.

### Bendall’s documentary findings

In *Queer Japan*, Bendall reports that approximately nine of the 32 subjects used sentence-final particles in the analyzed segments. *Ne* was the most frequent, with three tokens; *kana* occurred twice; and *no*, *wa*, *de wa*, *yo ne*, and *sa* occurred once each in the reported analysis.

The sample is too small for distributional inference. It does, however, show that a contemporary queer documentary sample used both conventionally gendered and broadly neutral forms. Bendall’s data also contain no shōjo exposure measure, no comparison group, and no evidence that any form was learned from manga.

### Majority-use comparison: form and function

The general conversation studies provide a more substantial context for interpreting queer cases.

Chen’s Fukuoka corpus found that the conventional “female” forms were not simply women’s forms. Female speakers used masculine-associated forms in intimate, informal situations, while male speakers used forms such as *no* and *ne*. *Yone* helped close female peers seek agreement and solidarity; *none* could soften or frame information as shared. Regional forms such as female *yaro* and falling *wa* were linked to Kyushu and Osaka backgrounds.

The Sakura corpus found young men using *wa* to express emotion, make personal claims, withdraw playfully from a conversation, and tease female friends. The article interprets these uses through *amae*: confidence that an intimate addressee will tolerate self-indulgence, complaint, or teasing. Again, the particle is not directly feminine; it acquires gendered readings through cultural expectations about emotionality and intimacy.

Fukao’s Meidai corpus shows that young speakers use *wa* in disagreement, correction, empathy, joking, and humor. Among younger speakers, *wa* can be a way of expressing a strong feeling while maintaining enough distance from the addressee to avoid a direct face-threatening confrontation.

Jia’s comparison shows that even apparently simple forms such as *yo* and *ne* vary according to the part of speech before them and the historical corpus. This makes it unsafe to compare raw particle totals without controlling for syntactic environment.

Carpi and Iacus found that in Twitter data, *kashira* was not more frequent among female-coded accounts despite its strongly feminine prescriptive label. They also found apparent convergence toward neutral forms and cross-gender use of particles such as *sa*, *na*, *ze*, and *zo* in specific occupational or public-persona groups.

### Shōjo particles and actual particles

The shōjo corpora and actual conversation differ in three important ways.

First, shōjo manga uses sentence-ending forms as part of character design. A strongly feminine form can mark an older woman, aristocratic background, seductive performance, or narrative femininity. A mildly masculine form can mark youth, anger, independence, or a boyish persona.

Second, actual conversation uses particles as sequential resources. Speakers select them to seek agreement, emphasize personal information, repair a misunderstanding, tease, soften a disagreement, or display intimacy.

Third, manga often lacks audible intonation. A written *wa* in a speech balloon may represent rising Tokyo *wa*, falling Kansai *wa*, a fictionalized role-language form, or a stylized emotional ending. The form alone cannot determine the interpretation.

This difference means that a queer reader could encounter a particle in manga and recognize it as feminine or masculine without carrying that classification into personal speech. Alternatively, the reader could appropriate the interactional effect—assertiveness, intimacy, teasing, emotional emphasis—while abandoning its conventional gender association. The available research does not reveal how often either process occurs.

### Sentence-ending particles: judgment

The direct evidence supports the following findings:

- queer speakers use particles associated with both masculine and feminine styles;
- particle choice can index intimacy, group membership, emotion, authority, teasing, or stance;
- *wa* and *no* are especially sensitive to prosody, dialect, and discourse function;
- young majority speakers frequently cross prescriptive gender boundaries;
- queer speech is not a single alternative particle system.

What is missing is precisely the requested media comparison. No study reports the sentence-ending-particle distribution of queer Japanese young adults by high and low shōjo consumption. No study estimates whether shōjo readers use more *wa*, *no*, *yo ne*, *kashira*, *zo*, or *ze* in their own speech. No study controls for region, prosody, addressee, identity, age, education, or other media.

## 7. What the evidence shows about media influence

### Four claims that must be separated

The phrase “media influence” can refer to several different processes. The evidence supports some of them more strongly than others.

| Claim | Evidence status | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| Shōjo manga represents gendered language in a distinctive way | Partially supported | Corpus studies show genre-, age-, and character-role patterns |
| Japanese audiences recognize media role language | Supported | Kinsui’s recognition evidence and role-language analysis |
| Shōjo consumption is associated with queer young adults’ pronoun or particle use | Not established | No focal exposure variable or outcome comparison |
| Shōjo consumption causes adoption of those forms | Not established | No longitudinal, experimental, or controlled causal study |
| Shōjo consumption has no measurable effect | Not established | No adequately powered null-effect test |

The appropriate answer is therefore not “shōjo manga does not influence language.” It is that the requested effect has not been measured.

### Mechanism 1: circulation and recognition

The strongest media mechanism is representational circulation. Manga repeatedly presents forms together with visual design, personality, occupation, age, and social role. Kinsui’s work shows that native speakers learn to interpret these combinations. Ueno’s historical account shows how print media helped circulate ideologies of women’s speech. The recognition experiment shows that Japanese participants can match speech to character images at high rates.

This mechanism can explain why a reader knows that *wa*, *kashira*, *ore*, or *washi* evokes a particular kind of person. It does not show that the reader will use the form.

### Mechanism 2: selective persona construction

Miyazaki’s school ethnography and Abe’s queer ethnography show that speakers can select a form for a meaning that differs from its stereotype.

Sakura girls used *ore* for coolness, assertiveness, and independence rather than male identity. Abe’s lesbian-bar employee used *ore* when angry with an intimate customer but *jibun* with a newer interlocutor. Gaishi used *ore* while rejecting classification as either girl or man. Kazuki used *no* to construct group authority rather than femininity.

These cases show how a media-recognized form can become a resource for personal expression. They do not show where a particular speaker first encountered the resource. The same form could be learned from family, school, peers, television, anime, manga, regional speech, or interaction with a queer community.

### Mechanism 3: community-mediated uptake

A community can reinterpret forms after encountering them in media. Abe’s lesbian bars and the onabe club show that queer environments may create local norms of directness, solidarity, humor, or toughness. Sato and Ishida’s BL surveys show that media can give some queer respondents language for desires and relationships, although the study does not concern linguistic forms.

Community-mediated uptake is especially important for queer speakers because the relevant process may not be imitation of a character. A reader may encounter a form in a fictional representation, discuss it with peers, and use it in a local style whose meaning is specific to that community. The outcome would be neither simple media copying nor independent community invention.

No available study measures this chain for shōjo manga, queer Japanese young adults, pronouns, or sentence-ending particles.

### Mechanism 4: broader historical diffusion

Historical evidence supports a broad relationship between mass media and language ideology. Late-Meiji novels and magazines helped make particular feminine forms socially recognizable. Newspapers and magazines after the 1948 Ueno Incident exposed average Japanese people to the lives and linguistic practices of danshō, according to Abe’s historical analysis. Kinsui shows how manga established recurring fictional registers such as elderly-male language.

These examples demonstrate that media can alter what forms are available as social symbols. They do not establish a direct reader-level effect, and none concerns shōjo consumption by queer young adults.

### Alternative explanations

A shōjo-exposure association, if eventually observed, would have to be distinguished from several alternatives.

#### Identity and self-positioning

Speakers may choose a pronoun or particle because it expresses their current identity, stance, mood, or desired persona. A queer young adult who uses *boku*, *ore*, or *jibun* may be responding to gender discomfort, masculinity, non-binary positioning, anger, intimacy, or resistance to a feminine stereotype. Media may provide a recognizable resource without causing the underlying positioning.

The LGBTER account shows a pronoun choice explicitly attributed to discomfort with *watashi*, not manga. Miyazaki shows girls using *ore* for social meanings unrelated to male identity. These are direct counterexamples to a one-step media explanation.

#### Peer and community practices

A bar, friendship group, online community, or workplace may normalize forms that are not common in majority speech. Abe’s cases show that forms can be used to construct solidarity or group authority. The relevant influence may therefore be local interaction rather than individual media consumption.

#### Addressee and intimacy

The same speaker may use different forms with a researcher, a regular customer, a family member, a partner, or a workplace superior. Abe’s 20-year-old employee shifted from *jibun* to *ore* according to addressee and emotional state. Any exposure study that records only one interaction per speaker would risk misclassifying a style shift as a stable preference.

#### Register and formality

Women in the *Queer Japan* documentary used formal language more consistently than men, but the source also observed shifts as speakers became more comfortable with the filming crew. A first-person form such as *watashi* can reflect public or documentary formality rather than feminine identity. A particle such as *wa* can likewise be selected in a casual, humorous, or regionally marked register.

#### Region and dialect

Falling *wa*, *yaro*, *yona*, *yan*, and related forms vary regionally. A speaker from Osaka or Kyushu may use a form that a standard-language textbook labels masculine or feminine without intending that social meaning. Regional distribution must be controlled before treating particle use as a gender or media effect.

#### Age and cohort

The shōjo corpora, CEJC, Fukao, Chen, and Jia all show age or period effects. Older fictional characters use more strongly feminine speech; young actual speakers use more neutral or cross-gender forms; historical corpora differ from contemporary corpora. Exposure to manga may correlate with age, but age itself may explain the linguistic outcome.

#### Education, occupation, and social setting

University students, bar employees, office workers, performers, manga artists, and documentary participants occupy different linguistic environments. Education and occupation affect access to registers, peer groups, and public personae. They may also affect which manga genres are accessible or attractive.

#### Other media exposure

Sato and Ishida show that BL readers commonly consume multiple formats—manga, anime, novels, drama, film, and games. A person who reads shōjo manga may also watch anime, television variety shows, or social media content containing the same forms. Without measuring co-exposure, an observed association cannot be attributed to shōjo.

#### Selection and reverse causation

People may select media that already fit their identities or preferred styles. A queer reader who likes nontraditional gender expression may choose shōjo, yuri, BL, or specific titles because those media resonate with an existing identity or desire. In that case, the association would not show that shōjo caused the linguistic preference.

#### Observation effects

Documentary participants and interviewees know they are being recorded. The researchers in the queer-language studies also shape the interaction. Bendall explicitly discusses the observer’s paradox, and Abe’s cases show that closeness and setting affect speech. Recorded personal expression is not automatically equivalent to unmonitored everyday language.

### What evidence would alter the judgment?

The conclusion would change if a study found a defined sample of queer Japanese young adults with:

- a consistent age band and self-identification procedure;
- measured shōjo exposure amount, timing, titles, and subgenres;
- information about BL, yuri, shōnen, josei, anime, television, and social-media exposure;
- naturalistic speech or writing samples across more than one addressee and register;
- coded pronoun omission, pronoun form, particle form, prosody, function, and interactional context;
- comparison groups or within-speaker longitudinal data;
- controls for region, age, education, occupation, identity, peer network, and formality.

A high-exposure group that consistently differed after those controls would support an association. A longitudinal study showing adoption after exposure, especially with within-speaker change and comparison cases, would provide stronger evidence for contribution. A well-powered study finding no difference after the same controls would support a null effect. None of these designs is represented in the available evidence.

## 8. What the minority case reveals about personal expression

The queer case is valuable not because minority status automatically magnifies media influence, but because it exposes assumptions that majority-oriented studies often leave unexamined.

Traditional descriptions frequently assume that a female speaker is heterosexual, that a male speaker is heterosexual, and that gendered language directly reflects sex. Maree shows how that framework obscures queer speakers’ practices. Gaishi’s *ore* does not transparently mean “I am a man.” Kazuki’s *no* does not transparently mean “I am speaking like a woman.” Abe’s lesbian-bar cases show that masculine-coded forms can produce intimacy or toughness without a male identity.

Queer speakers therefore reveal that gendered forms are resources in an indexical field. Their meanings include:

- alignment or disalignment with femininity;
- rejection of being treated as a woman or man;
- construction of a local persona;
- intimacy and emotional exposure;
- authority within a group;
- humor, teasing, and solidarity;
- management of public and private selves.

This does not make queer Japanese young adults homogeneous. The available cases vary by lesbian, gay, trans, onabe, non-binary, bisexual, and unspecified positioning; by age; by region; by bar, documentary, workplace, or family context; and by addressee. A community category may be analytically useful while still containing sharply different practices.

The minority case also shows why linguistic variation cannot be read as proof of media influence. A queer speaker may use a form encountered in manga, but the form may be reinterpreted through peer practice. Another may reject it because it evokes an identity they do not want. Another may use it only while joking, performing toughness, or addressing an intimate friend. Another may omit pronouns almost entirely.

Media can contribute to the repertoire of recognizable choices. It does not determine which choice a speaker makes, what social meaning the choice has, or whether the choice is connected to the speaker’s media history.

## Conclusion

The evidence supports a clear but limited answer. Shōjo manga represents Japanese gendered language in a distinctive way: teenage female characters are often given neutral or mildly masculine sentence-ending patterns, while *ore* and *boku* remain concentrated among male characters. Strongly feminine forms are used selectively for age, elegance, authority, emotion, romance, or other character effects. Actual Japanese conversation differs from both this fictional pattern and prescriptive textbook categories, with frequent omission, cross-gender usage, regional variation, and context-sensitive functions.

Queer Japanese speakers provide especially strong evidence that pronouns and particles index stance, intimacy, group membership, and persona rather than fixed gender identity. But no available study measures shōjo consumption among queer Japanese young adults together with their pronoun and sentence-ending-particle use. The literature therefore establishes representational patterns and plausible mechanisms of recognition, circulation, and selective appropriation—not a measured media effect.

The most defensible judgment is that shōjo manga may supply socially legible linguistic resources for personal expression, but whether greater consumption changes queer Japanese young adults’ pronoun or particle choices remains empirically undetermined.
